World.title: Última hora de la entrada de inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | El Poder Judicial ve necesario reforzar los juzgados de Ceuta por la crisis migratoria
World.content:
El Poder Judicial ve necesario reforzar los juzgados de Ceuta para hacer frente a la crisis migratoria

El Consejo General del Poder Judicial (CGPJ) advierte de que la entrada masiva de 80.000 migrantes en Ceuta los pasados 30 y 31 de julio ha afectado “de manera extraordinaria al desarrollo del servicio público de justicia, especialmente a la Sección Civil y de Instrucción del Tribunal de Instancia y, especialmente, a la prestación del servicio de guardia”, según indican en una nota difundida tras la reunión de la Comisión Permanente del Poder Judicial. El Consejo pone de manifiesto que es “necesario implementar una comisión de servicio de un juez o magistrado para apoyar al Servicio de Guardia de las plazas de Instrucción de Ceuta, así como otra comisión de servicios específica para la plaza con competencia en materia de Violencia Sobre la Mujer para la tramitación de los delitos de abusos sexual”.

El órgano de gobierno de los jueces también traslada la “necesidad de incrementar el personal experimentado” en los juzgados de manera temporal, tanto de funcionarios como de un letrado de la administración de la justicia hasta la superación de la crisis. En concreto, el refuerzo sería de un gestor, dos tramitadores y un auxilio judicial. El CGPJ indica también que ha trasladado al Ministerio de la Presidencia, Justicia y Relaciones con las Cortes la necesidad de “incorporar dos intérpretes y un servicio urgente de tasación pericial para el servicio de guardia”. (Efe)

World.title: Begur: el pueblo de Girona en el que se para el reloj
World.content:
Este enclave del Baix Empordà ha logrado conservar la magia de sus playas y calas, goza de algunas de las mejores propuestas culinarias del territorio y atrae por igual a locales y foráneos, permaneciendo en un ventajoso segundo plano a la hora de atraer al turismo masivo

Begur es una localidad catalana cuya fundación los historiadores acostumbran a situar en 1019, con la construcción del castillo de la localidad, aunque sus inicios datan de la época feudal. Ubicada a apenas 30 kilómetros de Girona, esta joya del Baix Empordà consigue permanecer alejada durante gran parte del año de las rutas turísticas masificadas que recorren parajes como Barcelona, la siempre bulliciosa Costa Brava o ciertas zonas del Empordà. Conserva además intacta su capacidad para sorprender al viajero y acumula un buen número de razones que obligan al habitual a seguir volviendo a su calma chicha. En verano la cosa cambia y la población, de apenas 4.000 habitantes, se multiplica por diez, pero, aun así, el pueblo se las ingenia para seguir siendo (relativamente) tranquilo.

Sa Punta, un establecimiento familiar totalmente remodelado de la mano de un grupo de empresarios encabezados por Daniela McLean —ideóloga del proyecto y con amplia experiencia en leyendas de la hostelería de lujo como el Palace Hôtel de Crillon, en París, o el grupo Peninsula Hotels—, se ha convertido en uno de los grandes imanes de esta localidad de cielos limpios y carácter familiar, con su apariencia de casa señorial en cuyo interior se esconde el espíritu de una beach house pensada para apagar el móvil, desenchufar el ordenador y vivir como si el mundo exterior hubiera decidido dejarnos en paz durante unos días.

Más información 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde

El jardín del hotel Sa Punta, en Begur.

Este hotel cuenta con 36 habitaciones, un spa, un restaurante con vocación transversal y sin delirios de grandeza (hay arroces, pero también hamburguesas), una piscina perfecta para los que desean ponerse en remojo en lugar de encaminarse hacia la playa y un entorno donde predomina el verde y una tranquilidad casi desconcertante, teniendo en cuenta los desquiciantes parámetros urbanitas. “Estamos en un lugar emblemático, rodeado de campos, de viñedos y de rutas ideales para darse una vuelta en bici o un buen paseo. Es un hotel muy tranquilo porque hacemos yoga y es solo para adultos. Siempre digo que es un hotel que transmite calma: pensado para desconectar totalmente del estrés. Por eso muchas veces insistimos en lo de la beach house para explicar por qué esto no es un hotel de lujo al uso ni un cuatro estrellas convencional”, explica Sandra Julià, la directora del establecimiento. “Tampoco estamos en primera línea de mar, aunque en cinco minutos puedas plantarte en la playa. Es una zona más elevada, así que tenemos unas vistas preciosas, pero con un ambiente mucho más íntimo”, añade sobre este establecimiento que abre de abril a octubre para adaptarse a las necesidades y deseos de su clientela.

La dificultad de acceder a Begur si uno no dispone de coche (el transporte público funciona en la temporada estival, pero sigue siendo complejo acceder al pueblo) se ha convertido, paradójicamente, en una de las ventajas de la localidad. “Totalmente. Lo cierto es que la gran mayoría de nuestros clientes necesitan coche para llegar hasta aquí y está claro que, si fuera accesible con el tren, el autobús y el transporte público, sería muy diferente. Y no solo para el hotel, para toda la zona. La movilidad aquí ya es complicada. Es cierto que a Begur y a Pals puedes llegar en autobús, pero no llega el tren. Eso hace que sea un destino un poco más exclusivo”, confirma Julià.

Vista del castillo de Begur. BORIS STROUJKO (Alamy / Cordon Press)

Más allá de las virtudes de un alojamiento pensado para el reposo y la desconexión, si uno decide salir de Sa Punta, Begur ofrece una triada insuperable: gastronomía, paseos y un sinfín de destellos del pasado. “Creo que eso es precisamente lo que la gente viene buscando. Pueblos medievales como Pals o Peratallada, lugares históricos, una gastronomía increíble, el arroz de Pals y unas playas preciosas. Todas esas pequeñas calas llenas de encanto”, aporta Julià. Pero a pesar del innegable atractivo de la geografía y la idiosincrasia que recorre cada rincón del Baix Empordà, Julià reconoce que algunos de sus clientes vienen buscando cosas distintas: “Por supuesto, hay de todo y también nos gusta que sea así, tener muchos perfiles distintos y ser capaces de atenderles con la misma solvencia. Hay clientes que vienen únicamente a jugar al golf. Comen aquí todos los días y no quieren hacer nada más. O los ciclistas, que pasan el día entero sobre la bicicleta. ¡Hay de todo!”, sonríe.

Para que no queden dudas, la directora de Sa Punta deja claro que en el hotel se prioriza un enfoque centrado en el adulto. El establecimiento es un gran reclamo para el turista familiar, pero solo con adolescentes, ya que la edad mínima son 12 años. “Por eso tenemos muchas parejas o grupos de amigos que vienen a darse un homenaje culinario, y no hay niños, pero pueden traerse a sus perros… siempre que no pesen más de nueve kilos”, aclara.

El bar exterior del hotel Sa Punta.

Para ponerse las botas

Lo del buen comer es casi una obligación para cualquiera que visite este enclave gerundense. La oferta es amplia, el producto impecable y hay un buen número de lugares que parecen sacados de una de esas películas románticas en las que los protagonistas se ponen las botas con el mar de fondo. AlKostat del Mar (en el hotel Finca Victoria) es uno de esos paraísos: con un coloso como el chef Jordi Vilà, responsable de los fogones de dos templos barceloneses como el Alkimia y Alkostat al mando del establecimiento, esta se ha convertido en una de las citas imprescindibles para los amantes de la buena mesa.

El chef Jordi Vilà está al frente de AlKostat del Mar, en el hotel Finca Victoria.

“AlKostat del Mar es un proyecto que puede adaptarse al territorio y es totalmente permeable a la cocina local. Casi podríamos decir que por sedimentación se acomoda allí donde llega. Creo que hacemos una cocina muy fresca, muy de olores, muy de sabores, sencilla: catalana y tradicional, pero siempre con nuestro toque. Como trabajamos mucho con el producto de temporada, pues hay mucho tomate y mucho pescado a la brasa”, explica Vilà. ¿Un plato imprescindible? “La ensaladilla rusa a la brasa, en la que cada ingrediente pasa por las brasas antes de volver al plato. Creo que explica muy bien lo que hacemos”.

Por supuesto, la competencia es feroz y en la lista de los favoritos de la localidad también sacan la cabeza tótems como Cap Sa Sal y la sidrería Mooma. Si hay ganas de aventura, Far Nomo, en Llafranc, es otra recomendación de primera clase y localidades como Peratallada, Pals y Calella de Palafrugell también ofrecen una gran variedad de mesas en las que ponerse las botas.

Para los amantes de los paseos o las calas, Begur es un seguro de vida: en el camino que lleva de Aiguablava a Platja Fonda puede recorrerse uno de los tramos más bellos del Camí de Ronda de la Costa Brava. El sendero transcurre entre pinos y acantilados, enlazando pequeñas calas y miradores naturales con vistas al Mediterráneo. El recorrido culmina en la mencionada Platja Fonda, una playa de arena oscura encajada entre altas paredes rocosas que sigue conservando una atmósfera casi mágica.

Si uno se queda con ganas de más, nada mejor que apostar por la ruta que lleva desde Cap de Begur a El Semàfor, un recorrido menos conocido que permite adentrarse en una de las zonas más agrestes del litoral de Begur. Un sendero que llega a una antigua estación electro-semafórica (la mencionada, El Semàfor), inaugurada en 1891 para orientar a los barcos de la Costa Brava. En el extremo del Cap de Begur, el edificio se abre hoy como mirador privilegiado sobre el mar.

Con tanto paseo, piscina, bici, golf y banquete, puede que en algún momento apetezca la irremediable tentación del dulce: para eso existe la Pastisseria Pa de pessic, uno de esos sitios a los que hay que ir dispuesto a dejarse aconsejar. “Abrí hace unos seis años y aposté desde el principio por la pastelería tradicional, pero reduciendo un 20% el azúcar. Abro todo el año y, aparte de brazos de gitano, coronas y pasteles como el de requesón (con queso local) o tiramisú con ratafía, mi producto estrella es el buñuelo del Empordà”, cuenta Anna Ferret, que regenta este palacete del dulce en la localidad gerundense.

Uno de los rulos de nata de la la Pastisseria Pa de pessic, en Begur.

La directora de Sa Punta quiere ofrecer a los interesados un último aliciente: “Tenemos un plus, que es algo que a mí me gusta mucho, y es que existe un gran sentimiento de comunidad que a su vez se traduce en una gran dosis de solidaridad: Sa punta forma parte de Costa Brava Centre y yo conozco a la mayoría de los directores de hoteles cercanos. Si tengo un banquete y me faltan sesenta platos, se los pido al hotel de al lado. Siempre nos ayudamos y eso me parece extraordinario en los tiempos que corren”. “Supongo que también es un buen modo de resumir lo que es Begur: un lugar en el que nunca te faltará de nada”, remata Julià.

World.title: Amancio Ortega compra por 175 millones un edificio de apartamentos en Londres
World.content:
La valoración de los 15 inmuebles en la capital inglesa supera ya los 4.200 millones

El fundador y primer accionista de Inditex, Amancio Ortega, a través de su brazo inversor Pontegadea, refuerza su presencia en Reino Unido tras adquirir en Londres un complejo de apartamentos por 150 millones de libras (175 millones de euros). De esta forma, Londres se ha convertido en una de las ciudades favoritas de Ortega para invertir, con cerca ya de 15 activos inmobiliarios valorados en conjunto en más de 4.200 millones de euros.

Es la primera adquisición de Ortega en el mercado del residencial para alquiler en Reino Unido, aunque en este segmento ya realizó importantes inversiones en Nueva York, Boston, Chicago o Dublín.

En concreto, el complejo de apartamentos está localizado en el 219 de Baker Street, en pleno barrio londinense de Marylebone, según ha adelantado el medio inmobiliario Green Street News. Esta adquisición se cerró el pasado mes de febrero y ha trascendido ahora al aparecer en el Registro Mercantil británico. Para esta operación la empresa constituyó una nueva filial en el Reino Unido y financió la operación mediante un préstamo intragrupo. El multimillonario español invierte habitualmente en este mercado británico a través de Pontegadea UK o Pontegadea GB.

Reino Unido es uno de los países favoritos de Pontegadea para invertir. Así, su filial británica, Pontegadea UK, cifraba en 2.654,5 millones de libras (unos 3.160 millones de euros) el valor de sus activos inmobiliarios en 2025, un 10,8% más, según las cuentas anuales depositadas en el registro oficial de empresas y sociedades británico.

El valor de las propiedades de inversión de la sociedad a 31 de diciembre de 2025 ascendía a 2.700,3 millones de libras (3.158 millones de euros), un 12,8% más.

Esta nueva compra llega después de que el vehículo inversor de Amancio Ortega desembarcara en Australia de la mano del consorcio liderado por el fondo Macquarie tras completar el pasado viernes la adquisición del ‘holding’ logístico australiano Qube, en una operación valorada en 11.700 millones de dólares australianos (7.165,94 millones de euros).

Además a finales de julio, la firma se reforzó en Francia tras adquirir por 850 millones de euros el complejo de oficinas Capital 8 de París en lo que es la mayor operación inmobiliaria de oficinas individuales ejecutada en la Europa continental desde 2022.

Mientras que a finales de la semana pasada acordó la venta de su participación del 13,7% al Estado portugués en el operador de la red eléctrica Redes Energéticas Nacionais (REN). Una operación que se realizará con la transferencia de 91,7 millones de acciones a la sociedad estatal Parpública.

En Reino Unido, también el pasado año, Ortega adquirió por más de 90 millones de euros un almacén de Amazon en Liverpool, que está alquilada en su totalidad al gigante del comercio electrónico a largo plazo.

Pontegadea ha seguido inviertiendo en 2026 en ladrillo. Además de los citados edificios de Boston y París, en lo que va de ejercicio ha adquirido un edificio de oficinas en Chicago por 440 millones, o sendas naves logísticas operadas por Amazony Lactalis en Canadá por 215 millones.

World.title: Por Mónaco sin datos en el móvil ni wifi, la mejor manera de recorrer el Principado
World.content:
Del Casino de Montecarlo a la catedral, pasando por Le Rocher y el Palacio Principesco, esta pequeña ciudad-estado hay que pasearla sin distracciones

En mis artículos para El Viajero no suelo usar la primera persona. Sin embargo, en esta ocasión procede hacerlo, no tanto como aviso para navegantes, sino para que se entienda mejor lo narrado.

A lo largo de los últimos años he visitado en más de una ocasión el Principado de Mónaco, al que es muy fácil llegar con el tren que bordea la Costa Azul, hallándose, por ejemplo, a menos de media hora de Niza. Mi primera vez en la patria de Raniero y Grace Kelly vino precedida de un vendaval de optimismo. Recordaba consejos de profesores del pasado, bien felices de narrar al alumnado cómo esta ciudad-estado consta de unos dos kilómetros cuadrados de superficie total, lo que hace suponer un fácil dominio de ese espacio, poblado por poco más de 38.000 habitantes, de los cuales 9.600 son de nacionalidad monegasca.

Más información Viaje por la Polonia judía

Bien es sabido que las apariencias engañan. Mónaco, independizado de Génova desde 1297, no forma parte de la Unión Europea pese a sus contactos más que frecuentes con Francia e Italia. Este factor, a priori, no supone ningún problema, o al menos antes no preocupaba a ningún visitante por el hábito de ir, a lo sumo, con un mapa para orientarse por sus calles. Pero los tiempos han cambiado y ahora mismo para muchos turistas resulta imprescindible disponer de internet para caminar con garantías. En mi caso confieso que suelo usar los mapas digitales como brújula base, para, a continuación, prescindir del móvil y así poder mirar bien aquello que piso sin condenarme a la pantalla.

El problema es que en Mónaco no puedes ir tan suelto —el roaming gratuito de la UE no se aplica de forma automática por ley—, al menos si es tu primera vez en el Principado, donde un exceso de confianza puede costarte una gran frustración, como fue mi caso tras bajar del tren, sentirme satisfecho por alcanzar el Casino de Montecarlo, que es el nombre de uno de los cuatro barrios del centro de Mónaco pese a confundirse por todo el conjunto, y luego soltarme hasta, literalmente, perderme en una serie de avenidas sin ninguna referencia visual válida para rehacer el camino y recuperar la cordura del itinerario.

Lo más grotesco de esa experiencia fue que pude entender con rotundidad mi fracaso al subir una cuesta e informarme un cartel de estar en Beausoleil, pueblo francés que junto a Montecarlo forma una sola aglomeración urbana. A partir de ese punto respiré hondo gracias a las vistas, perfectas para situarme y pasear sin necesidad de datos ni de conexión wifi al comprender la morfología de la ciudad.

Exterior del casino de Montecarlo. David Gee (Alamy / Cordon Press)

La clave de todo estriba, sobre todo para caminar sin riesgo a extraviarse, en salir de la estación por el sitio justo, que siempre es la Rue Grimaldi, e ir hasta la Avenue d’Ostende, desde la que cualquier ruta es fácil, si bien recomiendo ascenderla e ir hacia el Casino de Montecarlo porque siempre es el mejor punto de partida al ser un icono alejado del resto que sirve como Kilómetro cero hacia los demás.

Mónaco legalizó el juego en 1854 y necesitaba un edificio de postín para atraer a buscadores de fortuna que quisieran combinar la osadía con el prestigio de ganar dinero en un marco de veras incomparable, como lo fue el casino desde 1878, cuando Charles Garnier, autor de la Ópera de París, le confirió su actual aspecto. Este templo mundial de la apuesta, inmortalizado por Stefan Zweig en la novela 24 horas en la vida de una mujer (1924), ha proporcionado ingentes dividendos a la familia Grimaldi, si bien en nuestro siglo su facturación no es decisiva para las finanzas del Principado.

Desde el casino, con una plaza dispuesta para transitar entre el lujo y la egolatría contemporánea del selfi, lo mejor es volver a la Avenue d’Ostende, parándonos en cualquiera de sus pequeños miradores para aprehender mejor por dónde nos movemos sin marearnos por la enorme densidad de edificios entre imposibles rascacielos y hoteles de la Belle Époque afeados por estos excesos constructivos. Al final la vista se habitúa a los mismos porque cada sitio tiene su propia belleza, aunque aquí siempre es más hermoso mirar a la izquierda para admirar el Puerto de Hércules del barrio de La Condamine, que rodearemos para llegar al otro espectáculo que la vista nos ofrece en esta panorámica: Le Rocher, o la roca en las alturas donde se concentran los distintos poderes monegascos.

Vista de Le Rocher, donde se concentran los distintos poderes monegascos. Westend61 (getty images)

La encrucijada hacia esta meta se ubica, valga la redundancia, en el cruce de la Avenue d’Ostende con su paralela dedicada a John Fitzgerald Kennedy, que da paso al Quai dedicado a Alberto I, con comienzo y final capitalizado por dos estatuas que honran a leyendas del automovilismo. La primera es de William Grover, mientras la segunda, ya en las estribaciones de las escaleras hacia Le Rocher, es un homenaje al campeonísimo argentino de la especialidad Juan Manuel Fangio, quien cosechó dos victorias en el Gran Premio más famoso del circo de la F1.

Monumento en recuerdo del piloto argentino de Juan Manuel Fangio, en Mónaco. Paul Quayle (Alamy / Cordon Press)

Desde esta estatua, una de las más fotografiadas de nuestro recorrido, disponemos de un pequeño abanico de opciones para escalar hacia la roca, aunque mi consejo es ir por las avenidas du Port y de la Porte Neuve para no repetir nuestros pasos y no aburrirnos cuando regresemos de esta expedición, que tiene como cumbre el Palacio Principesco en su homónima plaza, donde cada día, a las 11.55 en punto, se produce el muy vitoreado cambio de guardia de los Carabineros del Príncipe.

El Palacio Principesco, ubicado en la plaza homónima.

La primera piedra de la residencia real se puso a finales del siglo XIII, remodelándose hasta finales de la decimonovena centuria, cuando aún se rodeaba de una rica vegetación en los alrededores, poco a poco rebajada sin desaparecer del todo pese al crecimiento de estos aledaños, que en nuestra época mezclan lo esencial de cualquier centro urbano con un apabullante número de tiendas dedicadas a vender baratijas y souvenirs. Lo mejor, como sospecharán, es parar poquito en esos negocios y, aquí sí, caracolear por las callecitas sin temor a descarriarse porque todo queda cerca, de los miradores a la catedral, construida en 1875 y firmada por el arquitecto Charles Lenormand, con una blanquísima fachada que oculta un rico interior dividido en tres naves, a rebosar de obras de arte, muchas de ellas provenientes del anterior templo, demolido como preludio a su completa renovación de estilo neorromántico.

La catedral de Nuestra Señora Inmaculada, conocida también como catedral de Mónaco. Barry Winiker (getty images)

De la catedral —lugar de entierro del príncipe Rainiero III y la princesa Grace— al último hito de este pequeñísimo país median menos de 300 metros. Se trata del Museo Oceanográfico, impulsado por el príncipe Alberto I, cuya fama de gran navegante se simboliza por este legado, abierto al público en marzo de 1910 y dirigido a partir de 1957 (y durante más de 30 años), en coincidencia con el auge turístico, por el comandante Jacques-Yves Cousteau, fundamental para armar el aparato pedagógico de la institución, muy en consonancia con el transmitido en sus documentales televisivos que tanta popularidad le dieron durante la segunda mitad del siglo pasado.

Mónaco no encierra muchas dificultades para el visitante y puede saborearse al detalle en pocas horas con la virtud añadida de conseguir que muchos se sientan menos dependientes de la tecnología por esa carambola de no poder usar los datos del móvil como en la Unión Europea. Ahora que terminamos les confesaré que claro, seguro encuentran alguna red wifi disponible brindada por las autoridades, pero créanme, si prescinden de teclear su contraseña ganarán tiempo y el privilegio de poder andar con el cuerpo bien erguido y los ojos fijos en el horizonte, algo que, por desgracia, cada vez es menos habitual en cualquier latitud del planeta.

World.title: Holidaymakers warned not to bring home “destructive” beetle
World.content:
The Dutch food standards watchdog NVWA has urged returning holidaymakers not to bring back foreign invaders after a Japanese beetle was found in a freight shipment from Italy.

The insect was found dead in a plastic container that was being transported from a region of Italy where Japanese beetles are known to live.

The NVWA set traps in the container to see if any live beetles had crept inside, but none were found. But the agency told people coming back from southern Europe and transport companies to be alert and report any specimens they found.

“The NVWA is explicitly asking trading and logistics companies to be alert for beetles hitching a lift when they travel to or through the named areas,” the agency said in a statement.

“Do not in any event leave the doors and windows of your vehicle open for longer than necessary and try to check goods and packing for beetles before departure if possible.“

Japanese beetles are not considered a pest in their native country, where their numbers are controlled by natural predators.

But in recent years they have been spotted in Italy, Croatia, Switzerland, Germany and the Azores. The German province of Hessen is the closest area to the Netherlands with an established population.

They are regarded as highly destructive because they feed on a wide range of vegetation. Adult beetles will devour leaves and stems of plants, while their larvae eat grass roots and weeds.

The NVWA has also published advice on its website advising people how to tell Japanese beetles apart from similar looking native species.

World.title: Inflation making plant-based foods cheaper than meat and dairy
World.content:
Plant-based foods now cost less than meat and dairy equivalents at nine major supermarkets in the Netherlands, according to new research published by food organisation ProVeg.

“It’s remarkable that this is happening,” Martine van Haperen, nutrition and health expert at ProVeg, told DutchNews.

“It’s normally been very difficult for plant-based products to compete with animal-based ones. What we’re seeing now is that store brands like Albert Heijn have expanded their own-brand products, making them more affordable.”

The bigger driver, she said, is inflation. “Inflation has hit animal products much harder than plant-based ones, and that is because animal products require much more resources to be produced.”

Cheaper across the board

ProVeg, which has tracked the price gap since 2022, compared the cheapest plant-based version of each product with the cheapest animal one, priced per kilo, at nine chains in late April.

A basic basket of six items stocked everywhere – mince, burgers, butter, milk, yoghurt and cheese – was cheaper in its plant-based form at every chain, by around 18% on average.

Shoppers buying staples such as mince and milk can save up to 30%, the organisation said, with the widest gaps at Plus and Dirk and the narrowest at the organic chain Ekoplaza. Plant-based butter came in 48% cheaper.

The plant-based versions of some products remain far more expensive, however: mayonnaise costs almost four times as much as the animal version, while vegan yoghurt and kwark are both more than double the price.

The bigger basket

ProVeg also compared a wider basket of 14 products – adding items such as sausages, shoarma and mayonnaise that not every chain sells in a plant-based version. On that fuller list the plant-based basket costs more at four shops: Dirk, Hoogvliet, Jumbo and Picnic. At Albert Heijn the two come out level.

Dirk is the odd one out, with its plant-based basics are among the cheapest of any chain, but its wider basket ends up 25% more expensive than the meat one. It stocks a plant-based version in all 14 categories – just not a cheap own-brand in every one, and those pricier extras drag the total up.

World.title: Police get stop and search powers after shootings in Zuidoost
World.content:
Police will be able to stop and search anyone for weapons in part of Amsterdam-Zuidoost for a week from Thursday, after a long series of shooting and gun threats that the city says often involve minors.

The mayor, police and public prosecutor have designated the H-buurt, the K-buurt and the Nelson Mandelapark a security risk area until August 27. Inside it, police can search people without having any specific cause for suspicion.

Authorities recorded 18 firearm-related incidents in the area between June 1 and August 1, ranging from threats made at gunpoint to shootings that left people wounded.

In one case on August 3, a shot fired during a confrontation passed through a wall into a child’s bedroom. A minor was inside the house at the time, reported local broadcaster AT5.

Second summer running

It is the second summer in a row that Zuidoost has faced such a regime. Last year’s designation followed the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old and was extended into September.

Extra police patrols had already been deployed this summer, the city said, but had not been enough to restore calm.

Controversial tactics

Preventive searching has been used in Rotterdam for a long time. It was introduced there in 2002 and now covers large parts of Rotterdam-Zuid.

The tactic is controversial, with opposition and coalition parties on Rotterdam’s council having accused the city of ethnic profiling. Stop and searches in Rotterdam require at least three police officers at every search to guard against it.

Amsterdam dropped preventive searching in 2015, deeming it ineffective. The city has still used it repeatedly over the past year, in the red light district, over New Year and now twice in Zuidoost.

World.title: Budget talks offer no clear route to majority for Dutch cabinet
World.content:
The cabinet has begun talks with opposition parties to try to secure a majority for next month’s annual budget, with prime minister Rob Jetten setting a target of August 28 to secure a deal.

The three-party coalition of D66, VVD and CDA is 10 seats short of a majority in the lower house and holds less than one-third of the seats in the Senate.

Commentators say the choice boils down to two options: either do a deal with the main left-wing party Progressief Nederland (PRO) – which was formed by the merger of PvdA and GroenLinks – or try to forge a majority on the right with JA21. But neither route is straightforward.

PRO leader Jesse Klaver told NRC this week that he supported the cabinet’s plans to invest €2.1 billion extra in defence and €1 billion in education.

But his party wants to force the cabinet to scrap its proposed €6.5 billion cuts to social security and raise the money instead through higher taxes on wealth and corporations.

Klaver said he was prepared to drive a hard bargain on the welfare cuts even though they are not due to be introduced until next year’s budget. His stance is backed up by the trade union movement, which has called a national transport workers’ strike for September 9 to protest against the reforms.

“We won’t let people live with uncertainty about cuts in the future,” Klaver said. “These need to be taken off the table this autumn.

VVD reluctance

The right-wing liberal VVD says the cuts are non-negotiable because they are not prepared to increase borrowing or let the budget deficit exceed the European Union’s 3% limit.

The VVD has been reluctant to negotiate with PRO, which it explicitly ruled out as a coalition partner during last year’s general election campaign and in the negotiations to form the current cabinet at the start of this year.

But the path to a majority on the right is even more complicated. Support from PRO would give the cabinet a healthy majority in the lower house and a near majority in the Senate, where the government needs to find just two more votes from smaller parties.

JA21 has nine seats in the lower house – one fewer than the number needed for a majority – but only two senators. The party wants the cabinet to cut welfare even further and reduce taxes, including the so-called “freedom contribution” proposed by the Christian Democrats (CDA) to fund defence spending.

JA21: “Constructive”

Its leader, Joost Eerdmans, said a video call with Jetten and the two deputy prime ministers, Dilan Yesilgöz of the VVD and Bart van den Brink of the CDA, had been “good and constructive” and further discussions would follow, without disclosing further details.

Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV group and the even more extreme Forum voor Democratie (FVD), which have 25 seats between them, are refusing to lend the cabinet any support.

DNA, the splinter group of former PVV MPs led by Gidi Markuszower, is willing to co-operate with the cabinet, but has not been invited to the negotiating table.

Markuszower has warned he will demand a high price for his party’s support: “People at home are crying out for more money in their pocket, lower costs, more houses, more secuity and less asylum, but the cabinet is failing on all fronts.”

BBB shut out

The farmers’ party BBB has also been left off the guest list for this week’s talks, even though the party has 11 seats in the Senate.

The BBB has been unhappy with the government’s plans to impose more limits on the agriculture sector in order to cut nitrogen pollution, which has triggered a new wave of farmers’ protests over the summer.

The party has been riven by defections in both houses in the last year, particularly the upper house, where five BBB senators have left the party, including two who switched allegiance to its arch-nemesis, the progressive liberal party D66.

Heinen absent

Even more intriguing is the fact that finance minister Eelco Heinen, who will present the budget when parliament reconvenes on September 15, is not attending the first two days of negotiations.

Heinen excused himself on the basis that the focus of the talks was to secure “political commitment” rather than discuss the details of fiscal policy, but Klaver remarked: “I can’t remember a previous time when the finance minister wasn’t there for the budget process.”

The Christian parties ChristenUnie and SGP, as well as the pensioners’ party 50Plus, are also due to meet with ministers on Wednesday.

World.title: Water board call in police after drought inspectors face threats
World.content:
Water authorities in Noord-Brabant have contacted police after inspectors received threats for checking whether local residents were breaking drought restrictions.

The Brabantse Delta water board, which covers an area centred on Breda stretching from the Maas to the Belgian border, has imposed a ban on taking water from streams and ditches between 9am and 9pm.

Inspectors have been using drones equipped with cameras to monitor fields since the ban was introduced a month ago. But staff who were named in a recent article on news website Omroep Brabant about their work have since ben subjected to threats.

Water board chairman Joris Bengevoord would not go into detail about the threats, but said a criminal complaint had been filed with police so they could investigate.

“It’s very serious and goes way too far,” he told NOS. “It’s not OK that they’re being threatened, which is why I’m speaking out as water board chair.

“We are doing this with the best intentions and I stand behind my staff. They are in the midst of it day after day.”

World.title: Do you know “Lucky”? Police can’t ID foreign man in Amsterdam
World.content:
Amsterdam cold case police are appealing for help identifying a man known as “Lucky” who collapsed on the street three years ago after suffering a suspected brain haemorrhage or stroke.

Doctors believe he subsequently developed aphasia, which makes communication nearly impossible. No one has been able to work out who he is or where he came from.

He now lives in a care home in Amsterdam Zuidoost and the only words he still uses are English ones – “nonsense” and “definitely” – which he uses to confirm or deny things. He spoke in an American or Canadian accent, the police say. Beyond that, he cannot talk or communicate at all.

Detectives first began looking into the case in 2023 but every line of inquiry ran into a dead end. The search then passed to the force’s cold case team, where two retired members, named as Ruud and Nel, are now volunteering to find out who he is. Presumably, somewhere his family or friends are looking for him.

A public appeal for information has garnered an “overwhelming” response, police say, with more than 140 tip-offs reported on the first day. A DNA and fingerprints search on the missing persons and deceased database returned no matches, VRT News reported the police as saying.

Two nicknames, conflicting clues

Digging into his former social circle, the investigators found that he belonged to a Buddhist community on Middenweg, in the east of the city, where he was known as “Lucky”. They also learned that he would occasionally have a drink at Soep en Zo, a café on Waterlooplein, where regulars knew him by a different name again: “Chris the Canadian”.

People who knew him think he may have come from the US or Canada because of his accent. He also may have had a past in Nepal, VRT News said.

Investigators say a lot of the information they’ve gathered is conflicting. “He was supposedly filthy rich, but at the same time he was wandering the streets of Amsterdam,” according to Ruud.

But what the investigators cannot understand is how a person could leave so little trace. “I simply cannot believe that nobody knows who this man really is,” Nel said. “Isn’t it strange that you could perhaps live under the radar in the Netherlands for 20 years?”

“Every person has the right to an identity,” Ruud stressed, “and that includes this man.”

Anyone with potential information on the case can report it to the police here.

World.title: Campaigners call for Amsterdam to pull plug on giant data centre
World.content:
More than 500 people have joined a campaign to stop a huge data centre being built in Amsterdam-Zuid, arguing that it will bring “zero benefits to the area”.

The Dutch government has introduced restrictions on the size of data centres in recent years following criticism from provincial and municipal governments about the strain on the electricity network. Data centres accounted for 4.6% of all electricity use in the Netherlands in 2024.

But the plans to build a 24,000 m2 facility on Amsterdam’s Science Park were submitted by US firm Equinix before the ban, which only applies to new developments, took effect in 2022.

Local residents have also become increasingly vocal in opposing the construction of data centres, while campaign groups Geef Tegengas and Extinction Rebellion both staged demonstrations this summer against a Microsoft project in Amsterdam Sloterdijk.

“There are already enough data centres to keep everything running. This is becoming overkill,” Dylan Bakker of Stop Datacenter Zuidoost told NOS.

Amsterdam city council, which wants to build 8,000 homes in Zuidoost to help relieve the national housing shortage, has attached extra conditions to the site, such as requiring the residual heat from the plant to be used for domestic heating.

Water and electricity

There are also concerns about the strain on water supplies, which have been exacerbated by the summer drought. Equinix said in its planning application that it would need 274 million litres of water a year for the first stage of the project, rising to more than a billion litres when the data centre is complete in 2036.

But the municipality says it would face legal action and penalties if it tore up the permit to build the data center at this stage.

Equinix has said it will only build one of four planned 60-metre data towers initially, until electricity grid operator Tennet can supply enough power.

Tennet warned earlier this year that the network was nearing capacity, leading to a six-month moratorium on new connections in Utrecht.

The complete campus in Zuidoost will consume 779 kWh of electricity a year, almost as much as all the households Amsterdam combined, which currently use 869 kWh.

Michiel Eielts, director of Equinix Benelux, argued that the data centres were an essential part of modern infrastructure. “Every house needs the internet. We need data centres for the growth of our companies, our public services and our security,” he said.

World.title: Dutch men face Argentina in World Cup hockey, women win again
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch men’s hockey team are taking on Argentina in their second World Cup group match on Tuesday, with the winners set to take a giant step towards the knock-out rounds.

Both teams won their opening matches comfortably, with the Netherlands beating New Zealand 5-1 in Amstelveen while Argentina overcame Japan by a 3-0 scoreline at the same venue.

The Netherlands and Belgium are co-hosting the tournament, 12 years after the World Cup was held in The Hague. On that occasion the Dutch women’s team won their tournament while the men lost in the final to Australia.

The women’s team are on the brink of reaching the quarter-finals this time after coming through a tricky tie against Australia to win 4-2.

Goalkeeper Anne Veenendaal was kept busy in the opening period as the Dutch had to defend seven penalty corners before taking the lead when Yibbi Jansen scored from a penalty corner at the other end.

Joosje Burg made it two midway through the second period, but Australia hit back almost immediately through Stephanie Kershaw.

After a goalless third quarter, the Australians equalised when Abigail Wilson converted a penalty corner, but Burg restored the lead with her second before Marijn Veen rounded off a fine move to make sure of the points.

In an intriguing subplot, the Argentinian men’s team includes Nicolas Keenan, the fiancé of Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by hockey.nl (@hockeynl)



Jetten wore an Argentina replica shirt as he cheered on his partner from the sidelines on Sunday’s match, but was evasive when asked by RTL which team he would be supporting on Tuesday.

“Hopefully it’ll be a draw so we don’t have to fall out at home,” he joked.

World.title: Poland “99% sure” fugitive opposition politician is in pro-Russian breakaway region of Moldova
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia. Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria. Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights. A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026 Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF. However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”. “I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region. "Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy" Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026 Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval. The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position. “If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week. “Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added. In his remarks today, Tusk said that Romanowski’s likely presence in Transnistria “speaks for itself regarding not only Mr Romanowski but the entire political group that covered up for and benefited from such people, and continues to cover up for them”. PiS politicians have largely avoided commenting, noting that it has not been confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. However, deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek last week admitted that, if Romanowski did trael there, he would have “crossed a line”. Nie wyprzedzajmy faktów – powiedział poseł PiS Zbigniew Kuźmiuk, pytany, czy Marcin Romanowski może zostać zawieszony w partii.https://t.co/IQzuS8Ad7O — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 14, 2026 Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government from 2019 until 2023, when the party lost power to a new ruling coalition led by Tusk. In 2024, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 11 crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group and using crime as a source of income. However, he instead fled to Hungary, where he was granted asylum by the then-government of Viktor Orbán, a PiS ally. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, his successor, Péter Magyar, promised to extradite both Romanowski and Zbigniew Ziobro, the former PiS justice minister who had also fled criminal charges in Poland and been granted asylum by Orbán. However, as Magyar was sworn in as the new prime minister, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains, and Romanowski disappeared, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians deny the accusations against them and claim to be victims of political persecution by Tusk’s government. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. He denies wrongdoing and calls the case political revengehttps://t.co/BXdQgWm61q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In his comments on Tuesday morning, Nowak said that prosecutors had found “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. Polish prosecutors are still, however, attempting to confirm Romanowski’s whereabouts and secure his extradition to Poland to face justice. He is subject to a European Arrest Warrant. However, that applies only in EU countries, and Moldova is not a member of the bloc. The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty). InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February. If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each. Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO — WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026 The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle. The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%. The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing. In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994. InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office. In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence. In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself. However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty. World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) without paying capital gains tax. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. To największa od lat zmiana dla indywidualnych inwestorów i największy projekt budowy krajowego kapitału napędzającego rozwój polskiej gospodarki. 🇵🇱 — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) July 3, 2026 The government estimates the scheme could result in about 74 billion zloty flowing to the Warsaw Stock Exchange by 2040. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. Poland’s WIG20 stock market index has hit its highest ever level, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. However, in all three cases, the capital gains tax exemption is conditional on withdrawing funds after reaching retirement age. Despite the Polish stock market’s strong performance in recent years, Poles’ direct participation remains modest. Shares make up only 2.9% of household assets, the equivalent of 3% of GDP. That is well below the EU average of 8.2%. By contrast, households’ cash holdings are equivalent to 11.5% of GDP, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). World.title: Polish PM confirms he wants his “right-hand man” to be made constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has confirmed that he will seek to have Maciej Berek, a government minister who stepped down this week and whom Tusk calls his “right-hand man”, appointed as a judge on Poland’s constitutional court. The move has generated considerable controversy given that Tusk’s ruling coalition has repeatedly pledged to “depoliticise” the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after the previous national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government appointed its former politicians to the court. At a press conference on Thursday, however, Tusk defended the idea, describing Berek as an “apolitical and nonpartisan” figure who would help “fix the Constitutional Tribunal” after it was rendered illegitimate by PiS. Premier @donaldtusk potwierdził, że @MaciejBerek – do tej pory minister ds. nadzoru nad wdrażaniem polityki rządu – będzie kandydatem na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. – To jeden z najwybitniejszych polskich prawników – uzasadnił szef rządu.https://t.co/RsKLhLjHhC — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) August 13, 2026 Berek is a longstanding associate of Tusk. During Tusk’s first period as prime minister, from 2007 to 2014, Berek was head of the Government Legislation Centre (RCL) while also serving as secretary of the cabinet. After Tusk returned to power in 2023, heading a coalition of parties ranging from left to centre right, Berek was appointed as a minister without portfolio and then, in 2025, was made minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of government policy. He has, however, been an extremely low-key figure, rarely speaking in public. Berek is also not a member of parliament, and indeed not even a member of any political party. On Tuesday this week, Tusk unexpectedly announced before a cabinet meeting that Berek, whom he called his “right-hand man”, was leaving the government in order to “move on to other tasks”. The prime minister did not say what those tasks would be, but multiple media outlets reported that Berek would be presented as a candidate to become a judge on the Constitutional Tribunal. Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). When Tusk’s coalition came to power, it promised to restore the legitimacy of the TK, including by “depoliticising” it. In 2024, it approved legislation that would have banned anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. However, the measures were referred by the then-president, PiS ally Andrzej Duda, to the TK itself, which subsequently declared them unconstitutional, meaning they did not come into force. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 At a press conference on Thursday, Tusk confirmed the rumours that he would seek to make Berek a TK judge. He called Berek “one of the most distinguished Polish legal practitioners, who has made his apolitical and nonpartisan nature a hallmark”. Berek has a doctorate in law and, between his stints in government, worked as an assistant professor in the department of constitutional law at the University of Warsaw. “For him, compliance with the law and the constitution has always been paramount,” declared Tusk. “I don’t know anyone better equipped, better prepared, to help rectify the situation we face with the flawed Constitutional Tribunal.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk w #Warszawa: Nie mamy żadnych innych interesów w tej sprawie. Zależy nam na naprawieniu Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, żeby nie był na smyczy prezydenta i PiS-u, tylko wykonywał swoją robotę. — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 The prime minister acknowledged that his government had tried to ban politicians from serving on the TK. But he said that Berek himself had recently told him that, “under the current political circumstances, we must do everything we can to remedy the situation” at the tribunal. “Since methods that are unconstitutional are being used from the other side, I must also demonstrate my determination and that we won’t give in to such methods,” added Tusk. Those remarks, in which Tusk also called Święczkowski’s leadership of the TK “embarrassing”, were a reference to the fact that the current PiS-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, and Święczkowski have refused to accept four new TK judges chosen by parliament earlier this year. “We have no interests in this matter other than to repair the Constitutional Tribunal so that it is not a tool and is not under the thumb of the president or PiS, but rather that it performs its work as objectively as possible,” said Tusk. World.title: Poland reintroduces VAT cut and daily price caps to lower fuel costs for drivers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has announced that, from Monday, it will reintroduce some of the measures that were used earlier this year to lower prices for consumers at petrol stations amid the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The package, known in Polish as CPN and which will be in place from 17 August until at least 31 August, includes reducing VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and introducing retail consumer price caps on fuels set daily by the energy minister. Announcing the measures on Thursday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said they should result in prices falling by around 1 zloty (€0.23) per litre. Currently, average retail prices are 7.29 zloty for 95-octane petrol and 8.09 zloty for diesel, according to Polish price monitoring service E-Petrol. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Polska będzie w absolutnej czołówce europejskiej, jeśli chodzi o najniższe ceny paliw. pic.twitter.com/ar3IZbzFHQ — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 13, 2026 Tusk acknowledged that CPN will entail “serious costs” for the state budget. When similar measures (which also, unlike now, included cuts in excise duty on fuels) were in place between the end of March and end of June, they cost the state an estimated 4.7 billion zloty. On Thursday, the prime minister renewed his criticism of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki for last month refusing to sign into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits this year. The government said that the tax, which would have raised an estimated 4 billion zloty, was intended to help cover the costs of fuel subsidies. The profits of many fuel companies have boomed during the crisis, with Polish state energy giant Orlen last week announcing record half-year results. Nawrocki’s chancellery, however, has argued that fuel companies would seek to pass the costs of tax increases onto consumers, thereby increasing prices. CPN was first introduced in March in response to soaring fuel prices in the wake of US and Israeli attacks on Iran and subsequent disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. CPN subsequently helped bring Polish fuel prices to among the lowest in the EU. Since the measures were withdrawn in June, prices at the pump in Poland have risen significantly, placing pressure on the government to again cushion the blow for consumers. E-Petrol reports that prices have recently started to fall, but remain well above the levels seen before the crisis. Economists at PKO, a major bank, wrote on Thursday that higher fuel prices in July, which stemmed from the expiry of CPN and an increase in global oil prices, were the main drivers of inflation accelerating from 2.5% in June to 3.0% last month. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector. It also saw its highest-ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets https://t.co/uhGWJVQvf3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 On Thursday, Tusk claimed that the reintroduced CPN would lead to Poland having among “the lowest prices in Europe”, helping “possibly millions of Polish drivers, on critical days, when they return from holidays”. But he also acknowledged that fuel would “still be expensive”. Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, however, criticised the government for what he claimed was a belated response to high prices.
